zones.label: Typical House in a Blackout
zones.summary: A conventional Minnesota house with thin insulation, leaky joints, and small dark windows loses its heat quickly once the furnace stops.
facts: With the furnace off, heat leaks out through thin layers, thermal bridges, and gaps, so the indoor temperature drifts toward the outdoor temperature (Chapters 3 and 11).
Air leakage speeds the loss: warm air escapes at the top while cold air is drawn in at the bottom by the stack effect (Chapter 4).
Cold interior surfaces lower the mean radiant temperature, so people feel colder than the thermometer suggests (Chapter 4).
A cold house in a Minnesota January puts occupants at risk and can freeze pipes (Chapter 21).

zones.label: Resilient House in a Blackout
zones.summary: The same house built with a continuous, airtight, well-insulated envelope and south-facing glass cools slowly and can collect sun with no power.
facts: Continuous insulation and air sealing slow heat loss, and a compact form has less surface to lose it through (Chapters 11 and 19).
South-facing glass admits low winter sun that floors and walls absorb, but this helps only when the sun is out (Chapter 19).
Warm interior surfaces keep the radiant temperature up, so people can be comfortable at a lower air temperature (Chapter 4).
Resilience is not a guarantee. Very cold nights and long outages still need a plan, and fuel-burning heaters, grills, and generators must never be used indoors (CDC).

zones.label: The Survivability Clock
zones.summary: A blackout is a race against time: how long indoor conditions stay livable depends on the building.
facts: Alex Wilson coined passive survivability in 2005, after Hurricane Katrina, for a building's ability to maintain life-support conditions through an extended loss of power, heating fuel, or water.
The Resilient Design Institute argues that passive survivability should be a baseline for residential codes.
This poster shows no number of hours. The time to unsafe conditions depends on construction, weather, and occupants, so it is estimated for each building.
Chapter 21: in a Minnesota January, a well-insulated and airtight building loses heat slowly and gives occupants more time before pipes freeze.

zones.label: Insulation
zones.summary: A thick, continuous thermal control layer slows heat flow, so the house cools slowly when the furnace is off.
facts: Insulation is the thermal control layer; its resistance to heat flow is the R-value (Chapters 3 and 11).
Continuous insulation outside the structure covers the studs, which reduces thermal bridging and keeps the structure warm (Chapter 11).
The minimum levels are set by code: see the adopted Minnesota Energy Code. A resilient design may choose to go beyond the minimum.
Insulation works only as well as it is installed: gaps and compressed batts leave paths for heat.

zones.label: Air Sealing
zones.summary: A continuous, sealed air barrier stops warm indoor air from escaping and cold outdoor air from rushing in.
facts: Moving air carries both heat and moisture, so a leaky envelope loses heat faster than insulation alone can save (Chapters 4 and 11).
Common leak points include the rim joist, gaps around windows and doors, penetrations, and electrical boxes and recessed lights in exterior walls and ceilings (Chapter 12).
A blower door test measures how leaky the enclosure is, so the work can be checked instead of assumed (Chapter 12).
A tight building needs planned ventilation for fresh air and moisture control (Chapters 4 and 19).

zones.label: Passive Solar Gain
zones.summary: South-facing windows let low winter sun heat the room, with no pump, fan, or power needed.
facts: Passive solar design uses south-facing glazing, thermal mass such as a concrete floor, and a compact insulated enclosure (Chapter 19).
At latitude 45 degrees N, near Minneapolis, the noon sun on the winter solstice stands about 21.5 degrees above the horizon, low enough to reach deep into a room (Chapter 19).
Glass loses more heat than an insulated wall and sun is not guaranteed, so gain helps only in good weather and must be balanced with night loss (Chapter 19).

zones.label: Daylighting
zones.summary: Windows and high clerestory bands light the rooms during the day, so occupants can see and work without electricity.
facts: Daylight from a side window usefully reaches about two times the window head height into a room (Chapter 19).
A clerestory, a high band of windows, spreads light deeper into a room while reducing glare (Chapter 19).
Winter days are short and cloudy days are dim, so lanterns or battery-backed emergency lighting are still needed after dark (Chapter 16 covers emergency lighting).
Windows that light the room should not give up the heat the insulation saves, so glazing area is a balance (Chapter 19).

zones.label: Natural Ventilation
zones.summary: Operable windows on opposite sides, and low and high openings, move air through the house with no fans.
facts: Passive survivability covers heat as well as cold: in a summer outage, opening windows lets a house shed heat without air conditioning (Wilson, Resilient Design Institute).
The stack effect lets warm air rise out of high openings while cooler air enters low openings (Chapter 4).
Fresh air still matters when sealed up in winter. Never run a generator, grill, or camp stove indoors, and keep carbon monoxide alarms working (CDC).
Outdoor air is only cooler when the weather cooperates, so natural ventilation is a supplement, not a guarantee.

zones.label: Shading
zones.summary: A fixed overhang blocks the high summer sun and still lets in the low winter sun.
facts: At 45 degrees N the summer noon sun is about 68.5 degrees high and the winter noon sun about 21.5 degrees, so a south overhang can do both jobs (Chapter 19).
A projection of about 2.4 feet shades a 6 ft south window at summer noon and leaves most of it in sun in winter (Chapter 19 worked example).
East and west windows are harder to shade because the sun is low there, so designers limit them (Chapter 19).
Shading and insulation limit temperature swings, which helps a building ride out a disruption (Chapter 21).

quiz.question: A January storm cuts power and fuel to a house with thin walls, gappy joints, and small windows. In which scene does the indoor temperature fall fastest?
quiz.explanation: Without insulation, air sealing, and solar gain, heat escapes quickly and the house drifts toward the outdoor temperature.

quiz.question: Which scene shows the same house keeping its occupants in safer conditions after the furnace stops, thanks to several measures working together?
quiz.explanation: An insulated, airtight envelope with south-facing glass slows heat loss and collects winter sun.

quiz.question: Alex Wilson coined a term in 2005, after Hurricane Katrina, for a building's ability to keep life-support conditions through an extended loss of power or fuel. Which region shows that idea as a race against time?
quiz.explanation: Passive survivability is about how long conditions stay livable, which depends on the building.

quiz.question: Which region deliberately shows no number, because the time until conditions become unsafe is different for every building?
quiz.explanation: The time depends on construction, weather, and occupants, so it has to be estimated for each building.

quiz.question: A thick, unbroken layer in the walls, roof, and floor slows conduction so the house cools slowly. Which strategy tile shows it?
quiz.explanation: Insulation is the thermal control layer, rated by R-value.

quiz.question: A blower door test finds leaks at the rim joist, around window frames, and at electrical boxes. Which strategy tile fixes that problem?
quiz.explanation: A sealed, continuous air barrier stops heat and moisture from moving with the air.

quiz.question: On a clear winter day, low sun enters south-facing windows and warms a concrete floor. Which strategy tile does this describe?
quiz.explanation: Passive solar design collects and stores the sun's heat with no mechanical equipment.

quiz.question: Which strategy tile lets people read and work in the house at noon with every electric light off?
quiz.explanation: Windows and clerestories light the room during the day without electricity.

quiz.question: During a summer heat wave outage, which tile lets a house shed heat through windows opened low on one side and high on the other, with no fans?
quiz.explanation: Cooler air enters low, warm air leaves high, and the stack effect moves air without power.

quiz.question: A deep roof overhang blocks the steep summer sun but lets the low winter sun reach the floor. Which strategy tile shows it?
quiz.explanation: Fixed overhangs use the different sun angles in summer and winter.
